description: The system BIOS/UEFI does not show a connected SSD or HDD in the storage device list, preventing the operating system from being installed or booted from that drive.
symptoms: Drive is missing entirely from the BIOS storage/boot device list
Operating system installer cannot find any drive to install to
Drive was previously detected and has now disappeared from BIOS
Drive is detected in a different system but not this one
possible_causes: Loose or faulty SATA or power cable connection
SATA port disabled in BIOS settings
Drive controller mode (AHCI/RAID/IDE) mismatch preventing detection
Drive itself has failed or is not receiving power
M.2 slot conflict disabling a SATA port sharing the same lane
diagnostic_questions: Is the drive connected via SATA or M.2/NVMe?
Have the cables been reseated or swapped to rule out a bad cable?
Was the drive working before, or is this a first-time installation?
Are there other M.2 drives installed that might share and disable this SATA port?

commands.purpose: View the list of detected storage devices and current controller mode within BIOS/UEFI
commands.expected_result: Drive appears listed with its correct model and capacity
commands.abnormal_result: Drive does not appear at all, confirming a detection-level problem

troubleshooting_steps.action: Reseat or replace the SATA data and power cables, or reseat the M.2 drive in its slot.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Loose or faulty cables/connections are the most common cause of a drive not being detected.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the relevant SATA port or M.2 slot is enabled in BIOS storage configuration settings.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Ports and slots can be disabled intentionally or accidentally, hiding the drive from detection entirely.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check whether an installed M.2 drive is sharing lanes with and disabling the SATA port in question, per the motherboard manual.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many motherboards disable specific SATA ports automatically when certain M.2 slots are populated.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the drive in another system or with another cable to determine if the drive itself has failed.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the problem is the drive hardware or this system's connections/configuration.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Update the motherboard BIOS to the latest version if the drive is a newer model that may not be recognized by an older BIOS.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Older BIOS versions sometimes lack support for newer drive controllers or larger capacities.

possible_solutions: Reseat or replace SATA/power cables or the M.2 module
Enable the disabled SATA port or M.2 slot in BIOS
Move the drive to a SATA port not shared with an occupied M.2 slot
Update the motherboard BIOS/UEFI firmware
Replace the drive if confirmed failed on another system
prevention: Consult the motherboard manual for M.2/SATA lane sharing before installing multiple drives
Use quality, properly seated SATA cables
Keep BIOS/UEFI firmware reasonably up to date
Handle drives carefully to avoid connector damage

description: Custom BIOS/UEFI settings, such as boot order, fan curves, or overclocking profiles, revert to default values every time the system is fully powered off and turned back on.
symptoms: Custom BIOS settings do not persist after a full shutdown
System clock/date also resets along with other settings
Settings persist through restarts but not full power-offs
Issue may be constant or worsen over time
possible_causes: CMOS battery is depleted or failing
CMOS battery is improperly seated
Motherboard fault affecting the CMOS memory circuit
Settings were not properly saved (Exit without Save used instead of Save & Exit)
diagnostic_questions: Does the system clock/date also reset along with other settings?
How old is the system, and has the CMOS battery ever been replaced?
Are settings being saved correctly with F10 or the Save & Exit option before leaving BIOS?
Does the issue happen after every shutdown or only after being unplugged for extended periods?

commands.purpose: Verify the correct save method is being used when exiting BIOS after making changes
commands.expected_result: Settings persist correctly after using Save & Exit
commands.abnormal_result: Settings still reset even after properly saving, pointing to a CMOS battery or hardware issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm settings are being saved using F10 or the Save & Exit option rather than exiting without saving.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Rules out simple user error as the cause before investigating hardware.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check whether the system clock also resets, which strongly indicates a CMOS battery issue.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: The CMOS battery powers both the clock and saved settings memory when the system is unplugged.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Replace the CMOS battery (typically a CR2032 coin cell) on the motherboard.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A depleted or failing CMOS battery is the most common cause of settings not persisting.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Reconfigure BIOS settings and save after replacing the battery, then test through a full shutdown cycle.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the battery replacement resolved the issue.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the issue persists after a battery replacement, have the motherboard inspected for a fault in the CMOS circuit.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A persistent issue after battery replacement suggests a deeper motherboard-level hardware fault.

possible_solutions: Replace the CMOS battery
Ensure settings are properly saved before exiting BIOS
Reseat the CMOS battery if it was improperly installed
Have the motherboard inspected if the issue persists after battery replacement
prevention: Replace the CMOS battery proactively every few years
Always use Save & Exit when changing BIOS settings
Avoid leaving the system fully unpowered for extremely long periods without occasional use

description: The small coin-cell battery on the motherboard that maintains BIOS settings and system time has failed or is critically low, causing configuration loss and possible startup warnings.
symptoms: System clock resets to a default past date on every boot
Warning message such as 'CMOS battery low' or 'CMOS checksum error' at startup
BIOS settings revert to defaults after each shutdown
System occasionally fails to boot until settings are reconfigured
possible_causes: CMOS battery has naturally depleted over years of use
Battery was of poor quality or defective from installation
System has been stored unpowered for an extended period
Battery contacts are corroded or making poor contact
diagnostic_questions: How old is the system and has the CMOS battery ever been replaced?
Does the system consistently show a CMOS-related warning at startup?
Does the clock reset every time, or only after extended power-off periods?
Is there any visible corrosion or damage around the battery socket?

commands.purpose: Check whether the system date/time has reset to a default value, a strong indicator of CMOS battery failure
commands.expected_result: Date and time are correct and current
commands.abnormal_result: Date/time has reset to a default such as January 1 of a past year, confirming battery failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off the system completely and unplug it from the wall outlet.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Ensures safety before opening the case and handling the motherboard.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Locate the CMOS battery on the motherboard (typically a CR2032 coin cell) and remove it carefully.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides access to replace the depleted battery.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Inspect the battery socket for corrosion or debris and clean if necessary.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Corrosion can prevent even a fresh battery from making proper contact.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Install a new CR2032 battery, ensuring correct polarity orientation.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A properly installed fresh battery resolves the underlying power issue causing settings loss.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power on the system, enter BIOS, reconfigure the date/time and any custom settings, then save.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms the fix and restores normal system configuration.

possible_solutions: Replace the CMOS battery with a new CR2032 cell
Clean corroded battery contacts
Reconfigure BIOS settings after replacement
Replace the motherboard if the battery socket itself is damaged
prevention: Replace the CMOS battery proactively every 3-5 years
Keep systems powered on or plugged in periodically if stored long-term
Use quality replacement batteries from reputable sources

description: The system displays a CMOS checksum error message during POST, indicating the stored BIOS configuration data is invalid or corrupted, and may load default settings or halt startup.
symptoms: Error message 'CMOS checksum error, defaults loaded' during startup
System boots but with BIOS settings reset to defaults
Error appears intermittently or on every boot
May be accompanied by other CMOS-related warnings
possible_causes: CMOS battery is failing or depleted
BIOS settings were corrupted by an improper shutdown or power interruption during a save
A failed BIOS update left configuration data in an inconsistent state
Physical damage or a fault in the CMOS memory chip on the motherboard
diagnostic_questions: Does the error appear on every boot or only occasionally?
Was there a recent power interruption, improper shutdown, or BIOS update?
How old is the CMOS battery, and has it been replaced recently?
Does entering BIOS, saving settings, and rebooting resolve the error temporarily?

commands.command: BIOS Setup > Load Optimized Defaults, then Save & Exit
commands.purpose: Reset BIOS to a known-good default configuration and save it cleanly to clear the checksum error
commands.expected_result: System boots normally afterward without the checksum error
commands.abnormal_result: Error persists or recurs quickly, indicating a CMOS battery or hardware issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Enter BIOS, load optimized/default settings, and save before exiting.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Establishes a clean, valid configuration to clear the immediate checksum error.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check whether the error recurs on the next boot after reconfiguring and saving.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Recurrence indicates the underlying cause has not been resolved, most likely the CMOS battery.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Replace the CMOS battery if the error recurs or the battery has not been replaced in several years.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A failing battery is the most common root cause of recurring checksum errors.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If a recent BIOS update coincided with the error, consider re-flashing the BIOS following manufacturer instructions.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An interrupted or failed BIOS update can leave configuration data corrupted, requiring a clean re-flash.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the error persists after battery replacement and a clean BIOS flash, have the motherboard inspected for a hardware fault.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Persistent checksum errors despite these fixes suggest a deeper motherboard-level issue.

possible_solutions: Load default BIOS settings and save cleanly
Replace the CMOS battery
Re-flash the BIOS if a failed update is suspected
Have the motherboard inspected for a hardware fault if the issue persists
prevention: Avoid interrupting power during BIOS updates or saves
Replace the CMOS battery proactively on aging systems
Use a UPS to prevent power interruptions during critical operations

description: An attempt to update or flash the motherboard's BIOS/UEFI firmware fails partway through, is interrupted, or results in the system failing to boot afterward.
symptoms: BIOS update utility reports an error or failure during the flashing process
System fails to POST or boot after the update attempt
No display output and no fan/LED activity change after a failed flash
Update utility hangs indefinitely without completing
possible_causes: Power interruption during the flashing process
Incorrect or corrupted BIOS firmware file used for the update
Incompatible firmware version for the specific motherboard revision
USB drive used for flashing was improperly formatted or prepared
diagnostic_questions: Was power interrupted at any point during the update process?
Was the firmware file downloaded directly from the motherboard manufacturer's official support page for the exact model and revision?
Does the motherboard support a BIOS recovery or dual-BIOS feature?
Is there any activity at all, such as fans spinning or LEDs lighting, after the failed update?

commands.command: Motherboard BIOS Flashback/Recovery procedure (varies by manufacturer)
commands.purpose: Attempt to recover the BIOS using the motherboard's built-in flashback or dual-BIOS recovery feature, if available
commands.expected_result: System recovers a working BIOS and boots to POST
commands.abnormal_result: No recovery feature available or recovery attempt also fails, requiring further hardware-level intervention

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check whether the motherboard has a BIOS flashback, dual-BIOS, or recovery feature and follow the manufacturer's documented recovery procedure.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many modern motherboards include a dedicated recovery mechanism specifically for failed BIOS updates.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify the firmware file used was the correct one for the exact motherboard model and revision, downloaded from the official manufacturer site.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Using an incorrect or corrupted firmware file is a common root cause of failed updates.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If a recovery feature is unavailable, check for signs of life such as fan spin-up, which may indicate the system is attempting a recovery boot.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some systems automatically attempt recovery from a backup BIOS chip or USB drive without an obvious recovery procedure.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If no recovery is possible and the motherboard has a socketed BIOS chip, consider a pre-programmed replacement chip or professional reflashing service.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A bricked BIOS chip that cannot self-recover may require external reprogramming or physical replacement.

possible_solutions: Use the motherboard's built-in BIOS flashback or dual-BIOS recovery feature
Re-flash using the correct firmware file for the exact board revision
Send the motherboard for professional BIOS chip reprogramming
Replace the BIOS chip if socketed and a pre-programmed replacement is available
prevention: Use a UPS to prevent power interruption during BIOS updates
Always download firmware directly from the manufacturer's official support page for the exact model/revision
Read the manufacturer's update instructions fully before starting
Avoid updating BIOS unless a specific fix or feature is needed

description: A user or administrator cannot access BIOS/UEFI settings because a previously set supervisor or system password has been forgotten, blocking configuration changes or boot device selection.
symptoms: Password prompt appears when attempting to enter BIOS setup
Entered password is rejected repeatedly
System may still boot to the operating system, but BIOS access is blocked
In some cases, the system itself will not boot without the password
possible_causes: Password was set by a previous user or administrator and not documented
Password was changed and the new one was forgotten or mistyped when set
Default or vendor-set password no longer matches documentation
Malicious or unauthorized password change by another party
diagnostic_questions: Was this password set intentionally by the current organization, or is its origin unknown?
Does the system still boot to the operating system despite BIOS being locked?
Is there any documentation or password manager record of the intended BIOS password?
Is this a laptop or desktop, as the reset procedure differs significantly between them?

commands.purpose: Check if the manufacturer provides a documented backdoor or reset code procedure for this specific model
commands.expected_result: A valid manufacturer-provided procedure grants access without hardware modification
commands.abnormal_result: No such procedure exists or it fails, requiring a hardware-level CMOS reset instead

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the manufacturer's support documentation for a model-specific password reset or backdoor procedure.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some manufacturers provide a legitimate way to reset or bypass the password without opening the case.

troubleshooting_steps.action: On a desktop, power off, unplug, open the case, and remove the CMOS battery for several minutes before reinserting.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Removing power from the CMOS memory clears the stored password along with other BIOS settings.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Alternatively, locate and use the motherboard's CLEAR CMOS jumper if present, following the motherboard manual.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: The clear CMOS jumper provides a faster, documented method to reset BIOS settings including passwords.

troubleshooting_steps.action: For laptops, where CMOS battery access is often difficult, contact the manufacturer's support for a proper reset procedure, as forcibly bypassing may void warranty.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Laptops often integrate the password differently, and improper attempts can cause further issues or void support.

troubleshooting_steps.action: After resetting, reconfigure BIOS settings and set a new password if desired, storing it securely this time.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Restores normal access and prevents a repeat of the same issue in the future.

possible_solutions: Use a manufacturer-documented password reset procedure
Remove and reinsert the CMOS battery to clear the password (desktop)
Use the Clear CMOS jumper on the motherboard (desktop)
Contact manufacturer support for laptop-specific reset procedures
prevention: Document any BIOS passwords securely in a password manager
Limit who has authority to set BIOS passwords
Use a consistent, documented password policy for BIOS/UEFI across the organization

description: The system does not respond to the usual key press (such as Del, F2, or Esc) intended to enter BIOS/UEFI setup during startup, booting directly into the operating system or displaying nothing.
symptoms: Pressing the BIOS entry key repeatedly has no effect
System boots directly to the operating system every time
No POST screen or manufacturer logo is visible to time the key press
BIOS entry worked previously and has since stopped
possible_causes: Fast Boot or Fast Startup is enabled, skipping the window to enter BIOS
Key press timing is off due to a very fast POST sequence
Keyboard is not being recognized early enough in the boot process (common with some USB keyboards)
BIOS entry key is genuinely different from what is being tried for this specific system
diagnostic_questions: Is Fast Boot or a similar quick-startup feature known to be enabled on this system?
Is a USB keyboard being used, and has a PS/2 keyboard been tried if available?
Has the correct BIOS entry key for this specific manufacturer and model been confirmed?
Did BIOS entry work previously, or has it never worked on this system?

commands.command: Windows Settings > Recovery > Advanced startup > Restart now, then UEFI Firmware Settings
commands.purpose: Use the Windows-based method to reboot directly into BIOS/UEFI, bypassing the need to time a key press
commands.expected_result: System restarts directly into BIOS/UEFI setup
commands.abnormal_result: Option is unavailable or fails, indicating a deeper Fast Boot or firmware access issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Use the Windows Advanced Startup option to restart directly into UEFI firmware settings, bypassing key timing entirely.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: This method reliably reaches BIOS/UEFI on modern systems regardless of Fast Boot or POST speed issues.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the Windows method is unavailable, try repeatedly tapping the entry key immediately from the moment power is applied, rather than waiting for a logo screen.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Fast POST sequences on modern systems can pass the entry window before a logo or prompt is even visible.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Disable Fast Startup in Windows Power Options if the system is fully shutting down and Fast Boot may be interfering.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Fast Startup can affect how the system initializes on the next power-on, sometimes reducing the BIOS entry window.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Try a different keyboard, particularly a PS/2 keyboard if available, or a different USB port.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some systems have inconsistent USB keyboard initialization timing during early boot, especially on certain ports.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the correct BIOS entry key for the specific manufacturer and model via official documentation.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Entry keys vary between manufacturers (Del, F2, F10, Esc), and using the wrong key will never succeed.

possible_solutions: Use Windows Advanced Startup to reboot directly into UEFI settings
Disable Fast Startup in Windows Power Options
Try a different keyboard or USB port
Confirm and use the correct manufacturer-specific BIOS entry key
prevention: Document the correct BIOS entry key and method for each system model
Prefer the Windows-based UEFI entry method on modern systems for reliability
Keep a wired, simple keyboard available for troubleshooting boot issues
keywords: boots straight to windows no bios

description: The system fails to boot, displays a security violation error, or cannot install certain operating systems due to a Secure Boot setting mismatch or configuration problem in BIOS/UEFI.
symptoms: Error message referencing a security policy violation or unsigned bootloader
Operating system installer refuses to proceed due to Secure Boot status
System that previously booted fine now shows a Secure Boot related error
Certain bootable USB drives or alternate operating systems fail to boot
possible_causes: Secure Boot is enabled but the operating system or bootloader is not properly signed for it
Secure Boot keys have become corrupted or were reset unexpectedly
A dual-boot or alternate OS setup conflicts with Secure Boot requirements
BIOS update reset Secure Boot settings to an incompatible default state
diagnostic_questions: What is the exact error message shown, and does it reference Secure Boot specifically?
Is the operating system or boot media designed to support Secure Boot, or does it require it disabled?
Was a BIOS update or reset performed recently before this issue began?
Is this a dual-boot system where one OS requires Secure Boot disabled?

commands.purpose: View and adjust the current Secure Boot enable/disable state and key configuration
commands.expected_result: Secure Boot state matches what the intended operating system or boot media requires
commands.abnormal_result: Secure Boot state conflicts with OS requirements, explaining the boot failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Identify the exact error message and confirm it relates specifically to Secure Boot.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Ensures troubleshooting effort is correctly focused rather than addressing an unrelated boot issue.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Determine whether the target operating system or boot media requires Secure Boot enabled or disabled.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Different operating systems and bootable tools have different Secure Boot requirements, and mismatches cause this exact error.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Adjust the Secure Boot setting in BIOS to match the requirement of the operating system being used.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly resolves the configuration mismatch causing the boot failure.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If Secure Boot keys appear corrupted, use the BIOS option to restore factory default Secure Boot keys.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Corrupted or missing keys prevent proper signature verification even with Secure Boot correctly enabled.

troubleshooting_steps.action: For dual-boot systems, research the specific Secure Boot requirements of each installed OS before finalizing the setting.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Ensures the chosen configuration does not break boot capability for the other installed operating system.

possible_solutions: Enable or disable Secure Boot to match the OS/boot media requirement
Restore factory default Secure Boot keys in BIOS
Update the bootloader or OS to a Secure Boot compatible version
Reconfigure dual-boot setup with Secure Boot considerations for both operating systems
prevention: Verify Secure Boot requirements before installing new operating systems or boot tools
Document Secure Boot settings changes for future reference
Test boot behavior after any BIOS update that may reset security settings

description: The system fails to recognize some or all installed RAM modules, showing a lower total memory capacity than expected, a memory error at POST, or failing to boot entirely.
symptoms: System reports less total RAM than what is physically installed
POST beep codes or error messages related to memory
System fails to boot with certain RAM modules installed
RAM works in one slot but not another
possible_causes: RAM module not fully seated in its slot
Incompatible RAM speed, type, or capacity for the motherboard
Faulty or damaged RAM module
Faulty or damaged RAM slot on the motherboard
RAM modules not installed in the correct slot configuration (dual/quad channel)
diagnostic_questions: Was this RAM recently installed, or did it work before and stop being detected?
Is the RAM confirmed compatible with the motherboard per the manufacturer's QVL (Qualified Vendor List)?
Does moving the RAM to a different slot change the behavior?
Are there any POST beep codes or on-screen error messages accompanying the issue?

commands.purpose: Check the total detected memory and per-slot population as reported by BIOS
commands.expected_result: All installed RAM modules are detected with correct total capacity
commands.abnormal_result: Detected capacity is lower than expected, or specific slots show as empty despite a module being installed

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and reseat each RAM module firmly in its slot, ensuring the retention clips fully engage.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Improperly seated RAM is one of the most common and simplest causes of detection failure.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test each RAM module individually in a single known-good slot to identify if a specific module is faulty.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the issue lies with a specific module rather than the system as a whole.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the same module in different slots to determine if a specific slot is faulty.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the issue lies with the motherboard slot rather than the RAM module itself.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify the RAM's speed, type, and capacity are compatible with the motherboard's specifications and QVL list.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Incompatible RAM may fail to be detected or cause instability even if physically installed correctly.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Update the motherboard BIOS if using newer or higher-capacity RAM modules that may need updated support.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Older BIOS versions sometimes lack proper support for newer memory modules.

possible_solutions: Reseat the RAM modules firmly
Replace a faulty RAM module identified through isolation testing
Use a different, functional RAM slot
Update the BIOS for better memory compatibility
Replace the motherboard if a slot is confirmed physically damaged
prevention: Verify RAM compatibility against the motherboard's QVL before purchase
Handle RAM modules carefully, avoiding static discharge
Ensure RAM is properly seated during any hardware installation or maintenance
keywords: system shows less ram than installed

description: The system fails to POST or shows an error indicating no CPU is detected, despite a processor being physically installed in the socket.
symptoms: System powers on but does not POST, with a CPU-related error LED or beep code
Motherboard CPU error LED remains lit continuously
No display output at all, with fans and lights active but no boot progress
System previously worked and stopped detecting the CPU after reseating or an upgrade
possible_causes: CPU is not fully or correctly seated in its socket
Bent or damaged pins on the CPU or socket (pin-based sockets)
CPU is incompatible with the current motherboard BIOS version, particularly for newer CPUs on older boards
Insufficient or improperly connected CPU power cable (8-pin/4-pin EPS)
Faulty CPU or motherboard socket
diagnostic_questions: Was the CPU recently installed, reseated, or upgraded before this issue began?
Is the motherboard's BIOS version confirmed to support this specific CPU model?
Is the CPU power connector (separate from the main 24-pin) fully and correctly connected?
Are there any visible bent pins on the CPU or in the socket?

commands.purpose: Read the motherboard's onboard debug LED or Q-code display, if present, to identify the specific stage of POST failure
commands.expected_result: Debug code progresses normally through POST stages
commands.abnormal_result: Debug code remains stuck at a CPU-related stage, confirming a CPU detection issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and visually inspect the CPU and socket for any bent or damaged pins.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Bent pins are a common and serious cause of CPU detection failure, especially after installation or reseating.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the CPU power connector (EPS 8-pin/4-pin) near the top of the motherboard is fully and correctly seated.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: This separate power connector is easy to overlook and is required for the CPU to receive power, distinct from the main 24-pin connector.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Reseat the CPU carefully following the motherboard manufacturer's installation guide, ensuring proper alignment.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An improperly seated CPU, even without visible damage, can fail to establish proper electrical contact.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check the motherboard manufacturer's CPU support list to confirm the current BIOS version supports this specific CPU model.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Newer CPUs on older motherboards sometimes require a BIOS update before the CPU is recognized at all, which can create a chicken-and-egg situation requiring a boot-compatible older CPU or a BIOS flashback feature.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If available, use the motherboard's debug LED or Q-code display to pinpoint the exact POST failure stage.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides more specific diagnostic information than a generic 'no boot' symptom.

possible_solutions: Reseat the CPU correctly in its socket
Properly connect the CPU power connector
Update the motherboard BIOS using flashback if supported, using a compatible CPU or USB method
Replace the CPU if bent pins or damage are confirmed
Replace the motherboard if the socket itself is damaged
prevention: Handle CPUs carefully to avoid pin damage during installation
Verify CPU/motherboard BIOS compatibility before purchasing a new CPU
Always connect both the main and CPU power connectors during builds
Follow manufacturer installation guides precisely

description: The system does not recognize an installed discrete graphics card, either showing no display output through the card's ports or failing to list it in Device Manager or BIOS.
symptoms: No display output when connected to the graphics card's video ports
Display works when connected to the motherboard's onboard video output instead
Graphics card does not appear in Device Manager or BIOS device lists
System boots but with reduced performance consistent with using integrated graphics
possible_causes: Graphics card not fully seated in its PCIe slot
Insufficient or improperly connected PCIe power connectors to the card
Monitor cable connected to the motherboard's onboard video output instead of the graphics card
Primary display output not set correctly in BIOS when both onboard and discrete graphics are present
Faulty graphics card or PCIe slot
diagnostic_questions: Is the monitor cable connected to the graphics card's ports specifically, not the motherboard's onboard video output?
Are all required PCIe power connectors (6-pin/8-pin) from the power supply connected to the card?
Is the graphics card fully seated and its retention clip engaged in the PCIe slot?
Does the BIOS have a setting for primary display adapter that might need adjustment?

commands.purpose: Check whether Windows detects the graphics card as an installed display adapter
commands.expected_result: Graphics card is listed and functioning without errors
commands.abnormal_result: Graphics card is missing entirely, or shown with a warning icon indicating a driver or detection problem

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the monitor cable is connected to the graphics card's video output ports, not the motherboard's onboard ports.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: This simple mix-up is one of the most common reasons a graphics card appears completely undetected.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and reseat the graphics card firmly in its PCIe slot, ensuring the retention clip engages.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An improperly seated card can fail to establish a proper connection despite appearing installed.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify all required PCIe power connectors from the power supply are firmly connected to the card.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Modern graphics cards require dedicated power beyond what the PCIe slot alone provides, and missing connections can prevent the card from initializing.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check BIOS settings for a primary display/graphics adapter option and set it to the discrete PCIe card if both onboard and discrete options exist.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some systems default to onboard graphics unless explicitly configured to prioritize the discrete card.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the graphics card in another system, or test another known-good card in this system, to isolate whether the card or the slot is at fault.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Determines definitively whether the problem is the card itself or the motherboard's PCIe slot.

possible_solutions: Connect the monitor to the graphics card's output, not the motherboard
Reseat the graphics card firmly in its PCIe slot
Connect all required PCIe power connectors
Set the correct primary display adapter in BIOS
Replace the graphics card or use a different PCIe slot if hardware failure is confirmed
prevention: Always connect the monitor to the discrete card when one is installed
Ensure adequate power supply capacity and connectors for the graphics card
Double-check BIOS display priority settings after installing a new graphics card
keywords: graphics card not showing device manager

description: A PCIe expansion card, such as a capture card, sound card, or network adapter, is not recognized by the system, either failing to appear in Device Manager or causing boot issues.
symptoms: PCIe device does not appear in Device Manager or BIOS PCIe device list
Device's expected functionality (capture, audio, networking) is completely unavailable
System may exhibit longer POST times or boot issues with the card installed
Device worked previously and stopped being detected
possible_causes: Card not fully seated in its PCIe slot
PCIe slot itself is disabled in BIOS or non-functional
Driver for the device is missing, outdated, or incompatible
Card requires supplemental power that has not been connected
PCIe lane conflict with another installed device, such as an M.2 drive
diagnostic_questions: Is the card fully seated with its retention clip engaged in the PCIe slot?
Does the card require supplemental power, and if so, is it connected?
Has the correct, current driver for this device been installed?
Could another installed device, such as an M.2 SSD, be sharing and consuming the same PCIe lanes?

commands.command: Device Manager > (relevant device category, or Other devices)
commands.purpose: Check whether Windows detects the PCIe device at all, even without a proper driver installed
commands.expected_result: Device appears listed, possibly under 'Other devices' if drivers are missing, but is at least detected
commands.abnormal_result: Device does not appear anywhere in Device Manager, indicating a detection-level rather than driver-level issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and reseat the PCIe card firmly in its slot, ensuring the retention clip is engaged.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An improperly seated card is a common and simple cause of complete non-detection.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify any required supplemental power connectors for the card are properly connected.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some PCIe cards require additional power beyond the slot itself and will not initialize without it.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check Device Manager to see if the device appears at all, even as an unknown or unconfigured device.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Distinguishes between a hardware detection failure and a driver-only issue.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Consult the motherboard manual for PCIe lane sharing that might disable or limit the slot when other devices, like M.2 drives, are populated.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many motherboards share PCIe lanes between certain slots and M.2 connectors, silently disabling one when the other is used.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Install or update the correct driver for the device once hardware detection is confirmed.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Even properly detected hardware requires a correct driver to function as intended.

possible_solutions: Reseat the PCIe card firmly in its slot
Connect any required supplemental power for the card
Move the card to a PCIe slot not sharing lanes with an occupied M.2 slot
Install or update the correct device driver
Test the card in another system to isolate a hardware fault
prevention: Review the motherboard manual for PCIe lane sharing before installing multiple expansion devices
Ensure all required power connectors are used for power-hungry expansion cards
Keep drivers updated for installed PCIe devices

description: An installed M.2 SSD does not appear in BIOS or the operating system, preventing it from being used for installation, storage, or boot purposes.
symptoms: M.2 SSD does not appear in BIOS storage device list
Drive does not appear in Disk Management or the OS installer
System may fail to boot if the M.2 drive was intended as the boot device
Drive was previously detected and has since disappeared
possible_causes: M.2 drive not fully seated or the retention screw not properly secured
M.2 slot configured for a different key type or protocol (SATA vs NVMe) than the drive supports
M.2 slot is disabled or shares lanes with a populated SATA port or PCIe slot
Drive itself has failed
BIOS does not support the specific M.2 drive without an update
diagnostic_questions: Is this a first-time installation, or did the drive work before and stop being detected?
Is the M.2 slot confirmed compatible with this drive's key type and protocol (SATA or NVMe)?
Is the M.2 retention screw properly securing the drive at the correct angle?
Are there other SATA or PCIe devices installed that might share and disable this M.2 slot's lanes?

commands.purpose: Check whether the M.2 drive appears in the BIOS storage device list and review M.2 slot configuration options
commands.expected_result: Drive is listed with correct model and capacity
commands.abnormal_result: Drive does not appear, confirming a detection-level issue requiring further investigation

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and reseat the M.2 drive, ensuring it sits at the correct angle and the retention screw is properly secured.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An improperly seated or unsecured M.2 drive can fail to make a reliable connection.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the M.2 slot supports the drive's specific key type (B-key, M-key) and protocol (SATA or NVMe).
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A physical or protocol mismatch between the drive and slot will prevent detection even if physically installed.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Consult the motherboard manual for PCIe/SATA lane sharing that could disable this M.2 slot when other devices are installed.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Populating certain SATA ports or PCIe slots can automatically disable specific M.2 slots on many motherboards.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the M.2 drive in a different compatible slot or another system if available.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Helps isolate whether the issue is the drive itself, the specific slot, or a lane-sharing conflict.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Update the motherboard BIOS if using a newer or higher-capacity M.2 drive that may require updated support.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Older BIOS versions sometimes lack proper support for newer M.2 drive models or capacities.

possible_solutions: Reseat the M.2 drive and properly secure the retention screw
Use a slot matching the drive's key type and protocol
Move conflicting SATA/PCIe devices to resolve lane sharing conflicts
Update the motherboard BIOS for better M.2 support
Replace the drive if confirmed failed via testing in another system
prevention: Review motherboard M.2 slot specifications and lane sharing before purchase and installation
Ensure the M.2 drive is properly secured with its retention screw
Keep BIOS firmware updated for newer drive compatibility

description: A drive or optical device connected via SATA is not recognized by the system in BIOS or the operating system, despite being properly connected.
symptoms: SATA drive or optical device does not appear in BIOS storage list
Device does not appear in Disk Management or File Explorer
Device was previously working and stopped being detected
Device works when connected to a different SATA port
possible_causes: Loose or faulty SATA data or power cable
SATA port disabled in BIOS or shared/disabled due to M.2 slot usage
SATA controller mode mismatch (AHCI/RAID/IDE)
Faulty SATA port on the motherboard
Device itself has failed
diagnostic_questions: Have the SATA data and power cables been reseated or swapped to rule out a bad cable?
Does the device work when connected to a different SATA port?
Is an M.2 drive installed that might be sharing and disabling this SATA port?
Was the SATA controller mode recently changed in BIOS?

commands.purpose: Check whether the SATA device is detected and review current SATA controller mode settings
commands.expected_result: Device is listed correctly under the appropriate SATA port
commands.abnormal_result: Device does not appear, confirming a detection issue requiring cable, port, or configuration troubleshooting

troubleshooting_steps.action: Reseat or replace the SATA data and power cables connected to the device.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Loose or faulty cables are the most common and easily resolved cause of SATA detection failure.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Move the device to a different SATA port on the motherboard.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the issue is a specific faulty port versus the device or cable itself.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check whether an installed M.2 drive is sharing and disabling this particular SATA port, per the motherboard manual.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many motherboards disable specific SATA ports when certain M.2 slots are populated.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the SATA controller mode in BIOS matches what the operating system expects (typically AHCI for modern systems).
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A mismatched controller mode can prevent devices from being properly recognized or cause the OS to fail to boot.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the device in another system, or test a known-good device in this system, to isolate a hardware fault.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Definitively determines whether the device or the motherboard port is at fault.

possible_solutions: Reseat or replace SATA data and power cables
Use a different SATA port on the motherboard
Resolve M.2/SATA lane sharing conflicts
Correct the SATA controller mode in BIOS
Replace the device or motherboard port if confirmed faulty
prevention: Use quality, properly seated SATA cables
Review motherboard SATA/M.2 lane sharing documentation before installing multiple drives
Avoid changing SATA controller mode after an OS is already installed without reconfiguring the OS accordingly

description: A specific PCIe slot on the motherboard fails to recognize any card installed in it, while other slots function normally, indicating a slot-specific rather than card-specific issue.
symptoms: No card is ever detected when installed in this specific slot
Multiple different, known-good cards fail to work in this slot
The same card works normally when moved to a different slot
Physical damage or discoloration may be visible on the slot itself
possible_causes: Physical damage to the PCIe slot, such as bent or broken pins
Slot is disabled in BIOS, whether intentionally or due to lane sharing with another device
Motherboard trace or solder joint failure affecting that specific slot
Slot is a lower-bandwidth or chipset-limited slot not intended for the type of card being tested
diagnostic_questions: Does the issue occur with multiple different cards, or just one specific card?
Does the same card work correctly when moved to a different PCIe slot?
Is there any visible physical damage to the slot itself?
Could this slot be sharing lanes with another populated device, such as an M.2 drive, per the motherboard manual?

commands.purpose: Check whether the specific PCIe slot is enabled and view its current lane allocation status
commands.expected_result: Slot is shown as enabled with appropriate lane allocation
commands.abnormal_result: Slot shows as disabled or with reduced/no lane allocation, explaining the detection failure

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test a different, known-good card in the problematic slot to confirm the issue is slot-specific.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Rules out the possibility that the original card, rather than the slot, is actually at fault.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the original card in a different, known-good PCIe slot.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Further confirms whether the card itself works fine elsewhere, isolating the fault to the specific slot.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Visually inspect the slot for any physical damage, bent pins, or debris.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Physical damage is a straightforward and visible cause of a completely non-functional slot.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check BIOS PCIe configuration settings to confirm the slot is enabled and review its lane allocation.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: The slot may be intentionally or automatically disabled due to lane sharing with another populated device.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the slot is confirmed physically damaged or has a motherboard-level fault, plan for motherboard replacement or use of a different slot going forward.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A genuinely faulty slot at the hardware level typically cannot be repaired without replacing the motherboard.

possible_solutions: Use a different, confirmed-working PCIe slot for the card
Enable the slot in BIOS if it was disabled due to configuration
Resolve lane sharing conflicts with other installed devices
Replace the motherboard if the slot is confirmed physically or electrically damaged
prevention: Handle cards carefully during installation to avoid slot damage
Review motherboard lane sharing documentation before populating multiple slots
Avoid applying excessive force when installing or removing PCIe cards

description: A specific RAM slot on the motherboard fails to recognize any memory module installed in it, while other slots function normally, indicating a slot-specific fault.
symptoms: No memory is detected when a module is installed only in this specific slot
Multiple different, known-good RAM modules fail in this slot
The same module works correctly when moved to a different slot
System may fail to boot or show reduced memory capacity depending on configuration
possible_causes: Physical damage to the RAM slot, such as bent or broken pins
Debris or foreign material lodged in the slot
Motherboard trace or solder joint failure affecting that specific slot
Retention clip on the slot is damaged, preventing proper module seating
diagnostic_questions: Does the issue occur with multiple different RAM modules, or just one specific module?
Does the same module work correctly when moved to a different RAM slot?
Is there any visible physical damage or debris in the slot?
Are the retention clips on this slot functioning and fully engaging the module?

commands.purpose: Check whether memory installed specifically in the suspected faulty slot is detected
commands.expected_result: Memory in the slot is detected and included in total capacity
commands.abnormal_result: Memory in that specific slot is not detected, confirming a slot-specific issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test a different, known-good RAM module in the problematic slot.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Rules out the possibility that the original module, rather than the slot, is actually at fault.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the original RAM module in a different, known-good slot.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the module itself works fine elsewhere, isolating the fault to the specific slot.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Visually inspect the slot for physical damage, bent pins, or debris, and clean gently if needed with compressed air.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Debris or minor physical obstruction can sometimes be resolved without requiring hardware replacement.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check that the slot's retention clips are functioning properly and fully engaging when a module is installed.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Damaged retention clips can prevent a module from seating deeply enough to make proper contact.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the slot is confirmed physically or electrically faulty, plan to use only functional slots and consider motherboard replacement if full capacity is needed.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A genuinely faulty slot typically cannot be repaired without replacing the motherboard.

possible_solutions: Use only confirmed-working RAM slots
Clean debris from the slot with compressed air if that was the cause
Replace the motherboard if the slot is confirmed physically or electrically damaged
Reconfigure RAM installation to only use functional slots while maintaining proper channel configuration
prevention: Handle RAM modules carefully during installation to avoid slot damage
Keep the system interior reasonably free of dust and debris
Avoid applying excessive force when installing or removing RAM modules

description: A specific M.2 slot on the motherboard fails to recognize any drive installed in it, while the drive works correctly in other compatible slots or systems, indicating a slot-specific fault.
symptoms: No M.2 drive is ever detected when installed in this specific slot
Multiple different, known-good M.2 drives fail in this slot
The same drive works correctly when moved to a different M.2 slot
Slot may show physical signs of damage or discoloration
possible_causes: Physical damage to the M.2 slot connector
Slot is disabled in BIOS or automatically disabled due to lane sharing with another populated device
Retention screw or standoff for this slot is missing or improperly positioned
Motherboard trace or connector failure specific to this slot
diagnostic_questions: Does the issue occur with multiple different M.2 drives, or just one specific drive?
Does the same drive work correctly when moved to a different M.2 slot?
Is the correct standoff screw present and positioned at the right length for this drive's form factor?
Could this slot be automatically disabled due to another populated SATA port or PCIe slot sharing its lanes?

commands.purpose: Check whether a drive installed in the specific suspected slot is detected and review its enable/disable status
commands.expected_result: Drive is detected when installed in this slot
commands.abnormal_result: Drive is not detected in this specific slot despite working elsewhere, confirming a slot-specific issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test a different, known-good M.2 drive in the problematic slot.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Rules out the possibility that the original drive, rather than the slot, is actually at fault.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the original drive in a different, known-good M.2 slot or another system.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the drive itself works fine elsewhere, isolating the fault to the specific slot.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the correct standoff screw is present and positioned at the proper length for the drive's form factor (2280, 2260, etc.).
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An incorrect or missing standoff can prevent the drive from seating and connecting properly.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check BIOS storage configuration to see if this specific slot is disabled, whether intentionally or due to lane sharing with another populated device.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many motherboards automatically disable certain M.2 slots when specific SATA ports or PCIe slots are also populated.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the slot is confirmed physically or electrically faulty, plan to use only functional slots and consider motherboard replacement if needed.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A genuinely faulty M.2 slot typically cannot be repaired without replacing the motherboard.

possible_solutions: Use only confirmed-working M.2 slots
Install the correct standoff screw for the drive's form factor
Resolve lane sharing conflicts disabling the slot
Replace the motherboard if the slot is confirmed physically or electrically damaged
prevention: Review motherboard M.2 slot documentation for lane sharing before installation
Use the correct standoff screws for each drive's form factor
Handle drives and slots carefully during installation

description: A specific SATA port on the motherboard fails to recognize any device connected to it, while other ports function normally, indicating a port-specific rather than device-specific fault.
symptoms: No device is detected when connected specifically to this SATA port
Multiple different, known-good devices fail when connected to this port
The same device works correctly when connected to a different SATA port
Port may show visible physical damage
possible_causes: Physical damage to the SATA port connector
Port is disabled in BIOS or automatically disabled due to M.2 slot lane sharing
Motherboard trace or solder joint failure specific to this port
Port is part of a secondary or add-in controller that is malfunctioning
diagnostic_questions: Does the issue occur with multiple different devices, or just one specific device?
Does the same device work correctly when connected to a different SATA port?
Is there any visible physical damage to the port itself?
Could an installed M.2 drive be sharing and disabling this specific SATA port?

commands.purpose: Check whether a device connected to the specific suspected port is detected and review port enable/disable status
commands.expected_result: Device is detected when connected to this port
commands.abnormal_result: Device is not detected on this specific port despite working elsewhere, confirming a port-specific issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test a different, known-good device connected to the problematic port.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Rules out the possibility that the original device, rather than the port, is actually at fault.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Test the original device connected to a different, known-good SATA port.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Confirms whether the device itself works fine elsewhere, isolating the fault to the specific port.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Visually inspect the port for physical damage or debris.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Physical damage is a straightforward and visible cause of a completely non-functional port.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check BIOS storage configuration to see if this specific port is disabled, whether intentionally or due to M.2 lane sharing.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Many motherboards automatically disable specific SATA ports when certain M.2 slots are populated.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the port is part of a secondary controller, check if a driver or firmware update for that controller resolves the issue.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some motherboards use additional chipsets for extra SATA ports that may need separate driver support.

possible_solutions: Use a different, confirmed-working SATA port
Resolve M.2 lane sharing conflicts disabling the port
Update drivers/firmware for a secondary SATA controller if applicable
Replace the motherboard if the port is confirmed physically or electrically damaged
prevention: Review motherboard SATA/M.2 lane sharing documentation before installing multiple drives
Handle SATA cables and connectors carefully to avoid port damage
Keep secondary storage controller drivers updated

description: The motherboard's CPU fan header does not provide power or control signal to a connected fan, resulting in the CPU cooler fan not spinning or not being recognized for speed monitoring.
symptoms: CPU fan does not spin at all when connected to the CPU_FAN header
System may show a CPU fan error or refuse to boot due to fan failure detection
Fan speed shows as 0 RPM in BIOS or monitoring software despite being connected
Fan spins normally when connected to a different header
possible_causes: Fan connector not fully seated in the header
CPU fan header itself has failed on the motherboard
BIOS fan control settings are misconfigured, such as an overly aggressive fan curve stopping the fan at low temperatures
Fan itself has failed and is not the header at fault
diagnostic_questions: Is the fan connector fully and correctly seated in the CPU_FAN header, matching the correct pin orientation?
Does the fan spin when connected to a different fan header on the motherboard?
Does a different, known-good fan also fail to spin when connected to this specific header?
Are BIOS fan control settings configured with a very low minimum speed or aggressive stop-at-low-temp curve?

commands.purpose: Check the reported RPM and configured fan curve for the CPU_FAN header
commands.expected_result: Fan shows a nonzero RPM reading consistent with normal operation
commands.abnormal_result: Fan shows 0 RPM despite being connected, confirming a header, fan, or configuration issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and confirm the fan connector is fully and correctly seated in the CPU_FAN header.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An improperly seated connector is a simple and common cause of a fan not receiving power.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Connect a different, known-good fan to the CPU_FAN header to test.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the header itself is the problem or the original fan has failed.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Connect the original fan to a different fan header on the motherboard, such as a system fan header, to test.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Further confirms whether the fan itself works, pointing definitively to the CPU_FAN header if it spins elsewhere.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check BIOS fan control settings for an aggressive curve that might be intentionally keeping the fan off or very slow at idle temperatures.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some fan curves are configured to stop the fan entirely below a certain temperature threshold, which can appear as a hardware failure.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the header is confirmed faulty, use a different available header temporarily and consider motherboard replacement or repair if the CPU_FAN header specifically is required for boot fan-detection.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some motherboards require a functioning CPU_FAN header specifically to avoid a fan failure warning at boot.

possible_solutions: Reseat the fan connector fully in the header
Adjust an overly aggressive BIOS fan curve
Use a different fan header if the CPU_FAN header is confirmed faulty
Replace a failed fan if confirmed via testing
Replace the motherboard if the header itself is confirmed damaged
prevention: Ensure fan connectors are fully seated during any build or maintenance
Set reasonable minimum fan speeds in BIOS to avoid stalling at low temperatures
Periodically check fan operation as part of routine maintenance

description: A motherboard's system/case fan header does not provide power or control signal to a connected fan, resulting in that specific case fan not spinning or not being monitored correctly.
symptoms: A specific case fan does not spin when connected to a particular system fan header
Fan speed shows as 0 RPM in BIOS or monitoring software for that header
Fan spins normally when connected to a different header
Other fans connected to other system fan headers work normally
possible_causes: Fan connector not fully seated in the header
The specific system fan header has failed on the motherboard
BIOS fan control settings for that header are misconfigured with too low a minimum speed
Fan itself has failed rather than the header
diagnostic_questions: Is the fan connector fully and correctly seated in the specific system fan header?
Does the fan spin when connected to a different system fan header?
Does a different, known-good fan also fail to spin on this specific header?
Are BIOS fan control settings for this specific header configured with a very low or zero minimum speed?

commands.purpose: Check the reported RPM and configured fan curve for the specific system fan header in question
commands.expected_result: Fan shows a nonzero RPM reading consistent with normal operation
commands.abnormal_result: Fan shows 0 RPM on this specific header despite being connected, confirming a header, fan, or configuration issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and confirm the fan connector is fully and correctly seated in the specific system fan header.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An improperly seated connector is a simple and common cause of a fan not receiving power.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Connect a different, known-good fan to the suspected faulty header to test.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the header itself is the problem or the original fan has failed.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Connect the original fan to a different system fan header to test.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Further confirms whether the fan itself works, pointing definitively to the specific header if it spins elsewhere.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check BIOS fan control settings specific to this header for an overly aggressive curve or zero minimum speed setting.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Some headers may be intentionally or accidentally configured to allow the fan to stop entirely at low temperatures.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the header is confirmed faulty, use a fan splitter from a working header or a different available header as a workaround.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Provides a practical solution to power the fan even if the specific header cannot be repaired without motherboard replacement.

possible_solutions: Reseat the fan connector fully in the header
Adjust an overly aggressive BIOS fan curve for that header
Use a fan splitter from a working header as a workaround
Replace a failed fan if confirmed via testing
Replace the motherboard if the header itself is confirmed damaged
prevention: Ensure fan connectors are fully seated during any build or maintenance
Set reasonable minimum fan speeds in BIOS for all headers
Periodically check all case fan operation as part of routine maintenance

problem: Fan Always Runs at Maximum Speed
description: One or more system fans run continuously at full speed regardless of actual system temperature, causing excessive noise even when the system is idle or under light load.
symptoms: Fan noise is consistently loud, even when the system is idle
Fan speed does not decrease even as temperatures drop after heavy use
Issue may affect one specific fan or all fans on the system
Fan speed control options in BIOS appear to have no effect
possible_causes: Fan is connected to a header without PWM/voltage control, such as a header wired for full power only
BIOS fan curve is misconfigured to run at 100% regardless of temperature
Fan itself is a non-PWM (3-pin/2-pin) fan connected expecting PWM control it cannot use
A temperature sensor reading is stuck high, causing the fan curve to always respond as if at maximum temperature
Motherboard fan control software conflict, such as competing BIOS and third-party utility settings
diagnostic_questions: Does this affect one specific fan or all fans in the system?
Is the affected fan a PWM (4-pin) or voltage-controlled (3-pin) fan, and does it match the header's control type?
Have BIOS fan curve settings been reviewed and configured intentionally, or left at a default that may run fans at maximum?
Is any third-party fan control software installed that might conflict with BIOS settings?

commands.purpose: Review the current fan curve configuration and reported temperature readings driving fan speed
commands.expected_result: Fan curve is configured reasonably, ramping with temperature rather than running at maximum constantly
commands.abnormal_result: Fan curve shows 100% duty cycle across all temperatures, or a temperature reading appears abnormally stuck high

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check BIOS fan control settings for the affected fan header and review the configured fan curve.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: An intentionally or accidentally configured 100% curve is a very common and simple cause of this symptom.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm whether the fan is PWM (4-pin) or voltage-controlled (3-pin) and matches the header's control type in BIOS.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A mismatch between fan type and header control mode can cause the fan to default to running at full speed.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Check for any third-party fan control software that might be overriding or conflicting with BIOS fan curve settings.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Competing software and BIOS control can cause unpredictable behavior, including fans defaulting to maximum speed.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Verify the temperature sensor associated with the fan curve is reporting reasonable values, not a stuck or clearly incorrect high reading.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A faulty sensor reading can cause the fan curve logic to always respond as though at maximum temperature.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Reconfigure the fan curve to a reasonable profile that ramps gradually with temperature.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly resolves the excessive noise issue while maintaining adequate cooling as temperatures actually rise.

possible_solutions: Reconfigure the BIOS fan curve to ramp gradually with temperature
Match the fan type (PWM/voltage) to the correct header control mode
Remove or reconfigure conflicting third-party fan control software
Replace a faulty temperature sensor if confirmed as the cause
prevention: Configure reasonable fan curves during initial system setup
Use consistent fan types matching header control modes throughout the build
Avoid running multiple conflicting fan control utilities simultaneously
keywords: fan always runs at maximum speed
case fan too loud always on

description: A connected fan spins normally and provides cooling, but the system, BIOS, or monitoring software reports its speed as 0 RPM or shows no reading at all.
symptoms: Fan visibly spins and provides airflow, but shows 0 RPM in BIOS or software
System may falsely trigger a fan failure warning despite the fan working
Speed reading is missing entirely rather than showing zero
Other fans on different headers report speed correctly
possible_causes: Fan is a 2-pin or basic 3-pin fan lacking a tachometer wire needed for speed reporting
Tachometer wire connection at the header is loose or improperly seated
Fan's tachometer signal wire has failed internally
Header itself is not properly reading the tachometer signal despite power being supplied correctly
diagnostic_questions: Is the fan confirmed to have a tachometer wire (typically a 3-pin or 4-pin fan, not a basic 2-pin)?
Is the fan connector fully and correctly seated in the header?
Does a different, known-good fan report speed correctly when connected to this same header?
Does this fan report speed correctly when connected to a different header?

commands.purpose: Check the reported RPM for the specific fan header in question while the fan is visibly spinning
commands.expected_result: RPM reading matches the fan's actual visible spin rate
commands.abnormal_result: RPM reads 0 or is missing despite the fan visibly spinning, confirming a tachometer signal issue

troubleshooting_steps.action: Confirm the fan has a tachometer wire by checking its pin count (2-pin fans typically lack this feature).
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A 2-pin fan without a tachometer wire will never report speed, which is expected rather than a fault.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Power off, unplug, and confirm the fan connector is fully and correctly seated in the header.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: A loose connection can specifically affect the thinner tachometer signal wire even while power still reaches the fan.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Connect a different, known-good fan with a tachometer wire to the same header to test.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Isolates whether the header can correctly read tachometer signals at all.

troubleshooting_steps.action: Connect the original fan to a different header known to correctly report fan speed.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Determines whether the issue lies with the fan's tachometer wire or the specific header.

troubleshooting_steps.action: If the fan lacks a tachometer wire and speed monitoring is important, replace it with a 3-pin or 4-pin fan that includes one.
troubleshooting_steps.reason: Directly resolves the reporting gap for cases where the fan hardware itself is the limitation.

possible_solutions: Reseat the fan connector to ensure proper tachometer wire contact
Replace a 2-pin fan with a 3-pin or 4-pin fan if speed monitoring is needed
Use a different, confirmed-working header for accurate speed reporting
Disable false fan failure warnings in BIOS if the fan is confirmed working despite no speed reading
prevention: Use fans with tachometer wires (3-pin or 4-pin) where speed monitoring matters
Ensure fan connectors are fully seated during any build or maintenance
Periodically verify fan speed readings match actual observed fan operation
